summary:
Sex between men is no longer a criminal offence in Singapore. Parliament repealed Section 377A on 29 November 2022, in the same sitting as a constitutional amendment reserving to Parliament, rather than the courts, the power to define marriage. Same-sex relations are lawful for men and women, and a Reuters feature in June 2023 recorded that the LGBT community felt safer after the repeal. Public-order law still reaches conduct in public places: Section 294 of the Penal Code covers obscene acts and carries up to three months' imprisonment, a fine, or both, and gay men were charged with soliciting in 11 cases between 1990 and 1994, with fines of S$200 to S$500.

Legal gender recognition depends on genital surgery, and a February 2025 stakeholder report on transgender health and well-being found the cost of the required procedures prohibitive for much of the community. A traveller whose documents, presentation or recorded sex do not align should expect the recognition framework to offer no straightforward route.

No form of same-sex relationship is recognised in Singapore: not marriage, not civil union, not domestic partnership. The Women's Charter provides that a marriage not between a woman and a man is void, and the constitutional amendment of 29 November 2022 reserves the definition of marriage to Parliament, leaving legalisation by simple majority open in future. Couples without recognition are excluded from the healthcare benefits, inheritance rights and social security benefits available to married couples. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship has no partner-recognition route, and a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status carries no spousal standing.

A workplace fairness law that took effect in January 2025 is Singapore's first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but it does not list gender identity or expression as protected grounds, so transgender staff have no statutory recourse against workplace discrimination.

The media regulator limits the promotion or glamorisation of the homosexual lifestyle on television and radio and imposes higher age ratings (NC16, M18, R21) on shows or films depicting same-sex sexual activity. In 2019 rapper Joshua Su (The G3sha) withdrew from a TEDx radio talk after being asked not to make sensitive comments about his sexuality.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Singapore, a structural gap that survives decriminalisation. Pride expression continues regardless: Pink Dot SG has been held annually since 2009, with record crowds of approximately 28,000 in recent years.

Gender-neutral toilets exist at Yale-NUS College and Tembusu College of the National University of Singapore. During Wikimania 2023 at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre (16 to 19 August 2023) a female toilet was temporarily converted to a gender-neutral one, drawing public backlash: the Facebook group We Are Against Pinkdot in Singapore threatened a boycott of Suntec and users sought petitions against the conversion. Pink Dot SG and the non-profit Oogachaga responded that gender-neutral toilets complement gendered toilets rather than replace them. Government representatives noted in 2014 that gay bars and clubs operate in Singapore.

On clinical care, Health Minister Gan Kim Yong wrote in May 2020 that the Ministry of Health expects doctors to practise evidence-based best practice and to respect patients' preferences and circumstances including sexual orientation, with complaints to the Singapore Medical Council as the recourse. No such complaint had been received from self-declared LGBTQ patients in the preceding three years.
tangentialFactors:
A May 2019 National University of Singapore study estimated 210,000 men who have sex with men in Singapore, more than double the previous estimate of 90,000, a population the authors described as at risk of a concentrated HIV epidemic.

A July 2025 clause of the radio broadcast code grouped homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden lifestyles, prompting a former radio DJ and actor to argue the grouping has no place in a post-377A Singapore and drawing calls for review.

A 2021 TODAY Youth Survey found 80% of respondents willing to work with LGBTQ people (6% disagreed), 75% willing to form close friendships (10% disagreed) and 58% willing to accept LGBTQ family members (18% disagreed).
localsOnly:
The February 2025 stakeholder report identifies four clusters of harm for transgender residents: a legal gender recognition process gated behind genital surgery whose cost is prohibitive; discrimination, abuse and restrictions facing transgender students; discrimination in the employment sector; and discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings.

In January 2006 the Ministry of Community Development, Youth and Sports granted S$100,000 (US$61,500) to Liberty League, an ex-gay conversion-therapy organisation. Activists pressured the group into returning the grant and it has been defunct since 2014.

Adoption by same-sex couples is generally not recognised. In December 2018 a gay Singaporean man won a landmark appeal to adopt his son, fathered through surrogacy in the United States. In January 2019 Social and Family Development Minister Desmond Lee said the government does not support the formation of family units with children of homosexual parents through institutions and processes such as adoption and would seek to strengthen adoption laws, a statement not yet made into law.

The Singapore Prison Service reported on 15 November 2023 that 10 transgender inmates were behind bars and that no cases of assault against transgender inmates had been recorded.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced account was located of how immigration officers at Singapore's checkpoints treat a traveller whose documents or presentation do not match recorded sex, or of screening practice specific to transgender arrivals. This is unresolved.

No trans-specific violence data for Singapore was located that would allow comparison against the general homicide rate. The absence of such figures is not evidence that targeting does not occur.

The January 2019 statement that adoption law would be strengthened has not been enacted; the operative position rests on the Women's Charter and on case law.

Enforcement of Section 294 is not disaggregated by gender identity in the available sources, and the soliciting prosecutions cited date from 1990 to 1994.

The refusal of registration to LGBTI organisations is documented, but the governing statutory basis and any appeal route are not sourced here.

Composite index scores for Singapore exist but aggregate de jure protection and lived-experience measures, yielding no discrete finding for a visitor.
